A persuasive case that Olaf Scholz values human rights can be built from his public commitments and concrete actions while serving as Germany’s chancellor:

- He has explicitly framed the protection of universal human rights as a core obligation of Germany and personally endorsed accountability mechanisms such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) in his address to the UN General Assembly on 20 September 2022. In that speech he said Germany has “an obligation to respect and to defend human rights at all times and in all places” and pledged support to the ICC and UN inquiries, and he publicly urged China to implement the UN High Commissioner’s recommendations on abuses in Xinjiang. ([new-york-un.diplo.de](https://new-york-un.diplo.de/un-en/2553516-2553516))

- His government enacted domestic rights-expanding legislation: the Self‑Determination Act, passed in April–May 2024 and entering into force in November 2024, replaced the 1980 Transsexuals Act and makes legal gender and name changes simpler for transgender, intersex, and non‑binary people—an unambiguous human‑rights advancement in personal autonomy and dignity. ([loc.gov](https://www.loc.gov/item/global-legal-monitor/2024-07-09/germany-new-self-id-act-for-transgender-intersex-and-nonbinary-individuals-enacted/?utm_source=openai))

- Under his chancellorship, Germany put into force and expanded the scope of the Supply Chain Due Diligence Act (LkSG)—a law that obliges companies to identify, prevent, and remedy human‑rights violations in their supply chains (covering firms with 3,000 employees since January 2023 and 1,000 since January 2024). This operationalizes respect for human rights beyond Germany’s borders. ([bafa.de](https://www.bafa.de/EN/Supply_Chain_Act/Overview/overview.html?utm_source=openai))

- At the European level, during his term the EU adopted the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) in 2024, requiring large companies to address forced labor and other abuses in their supply chains. Germany, as a member state, must transpose and apply it—further entrenching human‑rights due diligence in economic policy. ([consilium.europa.eu](https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/press/press-releases/2024/05/24/corporate-sustainability-due-diligence-council-gives-its-final-approval/?utm_source=openai))

- Germany has paired rhetoric with accountability practice: in 2025 German authorities executed an ICC arrest warrant and detained a Libyan suspect accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity for transfer to The Hague—demonstrating concrete cooperation with international justice. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/687cf39506a97ee2ebe3fa110217fa1c?utm_source=openai))

- His government has backed protection of people fleeing persecution and war at large scale. UNHCR reports that by the end of 2024 Germany was Europe’s second‑largest refugee‑hosting country (about 2.6 million refugees), and official German statistics recorded roughly 1.1 million arrivals from Ukraine in 2022 alone—evidence of a rights‑respecting protection stance. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/europe/about-unhcr/where-we-work/europe?utm_source=openai))

- Scholz has also raised human‑rights concerns directly with powerful partners. On his Beijing visit he said he pressed Chinese leaders on Xinjiang and stressed that human rights are universal, a position also reflected in his UN speech. Even critics of the trip acknowledged he brought up human‑rights issues. ([dw.com](https://www.dw.com/en/german-leaders-trip-to-china-raised-more-doubts-than-congratulations/a-63658657?utm_source=openai))

- The Federal Government’s 16th Human Rights Report (covering Oct 2022–Sep 2024) sets out his government’s efforts to promote equality, uphold feminist foreign‑policy guidelines, and fight impunity for serious violations—an institutional, sustained commitment under his chancellorship. ([auswaertiges-amt.de](https://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/en/aussenpolitik/menschenrechtsbericht-2691370?utm_source=openai))

Notes on nuance: On some politically sensitive issues (e.g., questions about possible ICC warrants related to the Israel‑Hamas war), Scholz and spokespersons emphasized judicial independence and the rule of law while avoiding hypotheticals before judges ruled. Regardless of the political caution in messaging, Germany continued to state support for ICC independence and cooperated with the Court in practice, as the 2025 arrest illustrates.
